alignment.note: The Greek opens with paratactic καί (and), which neither the Peshitta nor the Vulgate render here; the Syriac begins directly with the verb ܥܢܐ and the Vulgate with the relative Quibus, both absorbing the connective into syntax rather than translating it as a discrete particle.

The Greek articular subject marker ὁ together with the postpositive δέ (introducing slight adversative/continuative force) has no discrete counterpart in either the Peshitta or the Vulgate, both of which simply name Jesus as subject without the articular-particle apparatus.

Greek εἶπεν is a finite aorist coordinated asyndetically after the participle; the Peshitta renders ܘܐܡܪ with a prefixed waw, forming the idiomatic Semitic 'answered and said' construction, while the Vulgate ait stands alone, having already supplied respondens for the participle.
αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / the colon; the Vulgate marks the speech with punctuation rather than a dative pronoun, but the dative 'to them' is matched by Greek and Syriac.

Greek expresses the idea as a single compound noun σκληροκαρδίαν ('hard-heartedness') with the article and the genitive ὑμῶν; the Vulgate analytically separates it into duritiam cordis vestri ('hardness of your heart'), and the Peshitta likewise into ܩܫܝܘܬ ܠܒܟܘܢ ('hardness of your heart'), both unpacking the Greek compound into a construct/genitive chain.
The demonstrative ταύτην / ܗܢܐ / istud agrees across all three; the Vulgate's trailing colon (index 13) marks the close of this clause and the introduction of the ensuing citation.
